name: skew-detector
context: Aggregate throughput and cluster utilisation look healthy, yet one key, tenant, partition or worker carries a disproportionate share of the work and caps total throughput. Because parallelism in a partitioned system is bounded by the partition count and a partition is consumed by exactly one worker, no amount of consumer capacity fixes skew — the detector exists to make the unevenness visible before it is diagnosed as 'the pipeline is slow'. It measures per-partition distribution (records, bytes, latency, lag) rather than group aggregates, compares it against the median, and names the responsible key.
benefits: Separates a skew diagnosis from a throughput diagnosis: evenly spread lag means capacity, concentrated lag means key distribution
Converts an opaque 'consumers are busy' signal into a named hot key or hot partition that can be fixed in the data model
Runs continuously, so skew is caught at design time and before a replay or a connector snapshot turns a balanced workload into a spike
Provides the evidence needed to justify an irreversible change such as re-keying, splitting a topic, or moving a whale tenant
Surfaces skew that aggregate dashboards hide, including leader concentration across brokers, zones and storage paths
tradeoffs: Detection only observes what the runtime already reports — if per-partition or per-key metrics are not exported, there is nothing to detect on
Cheap counters on every partition and every key are expensive at high cardinality and are themselves a source of load
A detector that fires on transient bursts (backfills, compaction, rebalances) trains the team to ignore it unless it separates live traffic from replay traffic
Static skew thresholds based on a multiple of the median miss genuine skew in low-volume windows where the median is tiny
Diagnosis is cheap; remediation changes keying, which can alter ordering, compaction and downstream state semantics
use_cases: Kafka: one tenant is 40% of traffic, so its key pins a single partition to a single consumer
Spark: a sort-merge join whose skewed partition exceeds 5x the median partition size and 256 MB
Clickstream: a null or constant record key falls back to round-robin, destroying per-key ordering
Flink: a single keyed subtask dominating total processing time across an otherwise even deployment
Pre-migration rehearsal: proving a proposed re-keying actually balances load before applying it to production
avoid_when: The workload is naturally uniform and the per-partition metrics cost more than the risk they retire
Partition count is already the only parallelism bound and the key space cannot be changed
Replays, connector snapshots and partition reassignments dominate the measurement window — shape the workload, do not diagnose it
The system is request/response with no partitioned key space to skew
component_types: Distribution sampler: collects per-partition record counts, byte rates and produce/fetch latency
Lag comparator: compares per-partition consumer lag against the group aggregate and the per-group median
Key profiler: counts records per key over a sample window to name the hot key rather than just the hot partition
Skew classifier: marks a partition skewed when it exceeds both a size factor of the median and an absolute byte threshold
Remediation advisor: maps the observed bottleneck to a mitigation and states its hidden risk
anti_patterns: Alerting on group-aggregate lag, which reads as moderate whether 400k records are spread evenly or 399k sit on one partition
Adding consumers beyond the partition count and concluding the fix failed — the extras idle by construction
Increasing the partition count to fix a single hot key — the key still hashes to one partition, while the key-to-partition mapping changes for every existing key
Salting a hot key without a downstream de-salting merge, so results stay fragmented forever
Measuring only at the broker and never at the producer, missing that key choice is the root cause
design_principles: Measure the distribution, never the mean — a healthy average is the normal symptom of skew
Name the key, not just the partition — a partition symptom has a key cause
Separate live traffic from replay traffic before classifying skew
Report the mitigation's hidden risk alongside its benefit
Detection must be continuous and cheap enough to leave running
best_practices: Convert lag to age in seconds before reading it; count-based thresholds are meaningless across workloads
Compare every partition to the median, never to the mean, because the skew distorts the mean
Classify with two conditions — a factor of the median AND an absolute floor — so small partitions are not flagged
Confirm a hot partition's log-end-offset growth before blaming the consumer
Treat keying changes as a contract change: ordering, compaction and idempotency guarantees all move with them
references: Apache Spark, SQL Performance Tuning — Optimizing Skew Join (skewedPartitionFactor 5.0, skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes 256MB), https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/sql-performance-tuning.html
Apache Kafka, Streams DSL — GroupByKey, GroupBy, Repartition and co-partitioning rules, https://kafka.apache.org/43/streams/developer-guide/dsl-api/
Apache Kafka, Core Concepts — partitioning model and stream parallelism, https://kafka.apache.org/43/streams/core-concepts/
Apache Kafka, Operations — Monitoring and consumer rebalance protocol, https://kafka.apache.org/43/operations/monitoring/
